Wireless Communication Aided by Intelligent
Reﬂecting Surface: Active or Passive?
Changsheng Y ou, Member , IEEE and Rui Zhang, Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—In this letter , we consider an intelligent reﬂecting
surface (IRS)-aided wireless communication system, where an
active or passive IRS is employed to assist the communication
between an access point and a user . First, we consider the
downlink/uplink communication separately and optimize th e IRS
placement for rate maximization with an active or passive IR S.
We show that given the same number of IRS reﬂecting elements,
the active IRS should be deployed closer to the receiver with
the IRS’s decreasing ampliﬁcation power; while in contrast , the
passive IRS should be deployed near either the transmitter o r
receiver . Moreover , with optimized IRS placement, the pass ive
IRS is shown to outperform its active counterpart when the
number of reﬂecting elements is sufﬁciently large and/or th e
active-IRS ampliﬁcation power is too small. Next, we optimi ze
the IRS placement for both active and passive IRSs to maximiz e
the weighted sum-rate of uplink and downlink communication s.
We show that in this case, the passive IRS is more likely to
achieve superior rate performance. This is because the opti mal
active-IRS placement needs to balance the rate performance in
the uplink and downlink, while deploying the passive IRS nea r
the transmitter or receiver is optimal regardless of the upl ink or
downlink.
Index Terms—Intelligent reﬂecting surface (IRS), passive IRS,
active IRS, IRS deployment.
I. I NTRODUCTION
Intelligent reﬂecting surface (IRS) has emerged as a promis -
ing technology to reconﬁgure the radio propagation envi-
ronment in favor of wireless communications, by smartly
tuning the reﬂection amplitude and/or phase-shift at each o f
its large number of reﬂecting elements [1]–[3]. Moreover, I RS
is generally of light weight and proﬁle, thus can be easily
coated on environment objects to enhance the communication
performance in different wireless systems (see, e.g., [4]– [7]).

Quantum Darwinism demonstrates not only that preferred states are selected for their stability but also that information about them is broadcast by the same environment that causes decoherence and einselection. That environment acts both as a censor and as an advertising agent that disseminates information about pointer states while suppressing complementary information. Chapter 8 explores the implications and limitations of quantum Darwinism using models inspired by the structure of the Universe we inhabit. We perceive our Universe using light and other means of information transmission. We explore models that have a well-defined relation with our everyday reality, and where one can also selectively relax some of the idealized assumptions and investigate the consequences. Light is the communication channel through which we obtain most of our information. Fortunately, it is an ideal channel in the sense of quantum Darwinism, and simple but realistic cases are exactly solvable. Decomposition-Indexed Classicality: An A/R/F Framework for Observer-Dependent Quantum Experience
Authors/Creators
Almon, Ricardo
(Producer)
Contributors
Producer:
Almon, Ricardo
Description
This work develops a quantitative framework for
observer-dependent classicality
in quantum mechanics based on three operational functionals:
Redundancy (R)
,
Accessibility (A)
, and
Observer Flow (F)
. The A/R/F framework distinguishes environmental redundancy from the effective redundancy usable by a specific observer, models accessibility through a noisy-threshold aperture function, and introduces a continuity measure governing an observer’s capacity to integrate records over time. Classicality becomes a
decomposition-indexed property
, not a global feature of the universal wavefunction.
Applied to
Wigner’s Friend
and
Frauchiger–Renner
, the framework dissolves paradoxes by showing that cross-agent inferences fail precisely in regimes where effective accessibility is low. The paper outlines experimental signatures, including observer-dependent classicality thresholds and flow-disruption tests, offering a route toward
empirical constraints on observer-relative quantum structure
.
